title: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma: From Past to Future—A Comprehensive Review of Pathophysiology and Therapeutic Advances

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Hodgkin Lymphoma: Historical Context, Etiology, and Biological Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Immune Microenvironment and Biological Basis for Modern Therapy
subsections.content:
A defining biologic feature of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is the marked disparity between the scarcity of malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells and the abundance of non-malignant immune and stromal elements that constitute the tumor bed. This microenvironment is not merely reactive: HRS cells actively shape an immunosuppressive niche through recurrent 9p24.1 alterations involving CD274/PD-L1, PDCD1LG2/PD-L2, and JAK2, with additional induction through EBV-associated signaling in a subset of cases, thereby promoting T-cell exhaustion and immune escape ref [1], ref [2].

Histopathologic and spatial studies further show that PD-L1 expression extends beyond HRS cells to surrounding tumor-associated macrophages, creating a protective peri-tumoral niche in which inhibitory signaling is concentrated around the malignant cells ref [2]. Immune profiling has also demonstrated an exhausted effector T-cell compartment together with abundant regulatory CD4+ T cells, helping explain how a tumor with very few neoplastic cells can nevertheless persist and expand ref [1]. In pediatric cHL, similar biomarker patterns—including PD-L1 pathway activation and CD30 dependence—support the concept that immune contexture is central across age groups, while also informing translational trial design ref [4].

This biology provides one of the clearest mechanistic rationales for modern therapy in lymphoma. Because cHL is unusually dependent on PD-1 axis signaling for immune evasion, checkpoint blockade can restore anti-tumor immunity even in heavily pretreated disease, a principle validated by the durable activity of nivolumab and pembrolizumab and now being extended into earlier-line combinations ref [1]. More broadly, the microenvironmental dependence of cHL also underpins the success of other biologically targeted strategies, especially CD30-directed therapy and chemoimmunotherapy platforms designed to exploit immune reactivation while reducing long-term treatment burden ref [1], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Hodgkin Lymphoma: Historical Context, Etiology, and Biological Basis
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) occupies a distinctive place in oncology because it was recognized as a clinicopathologic entity long before its cellular and molecular basis was understood. In 1832, Thomas Hodgkin described a syndrome of progressive enlargement of the “absorbent glands and spleen,” establishing the historical foundation for what later became Hodgkin lymphoma ref [5]. Subsequent nineteenth- and early twentieth-century clinicopathologic work separated Hodgkin disease from tuberculosis and other lymphadenopathies and, eventually, linked its orderly nodal distribution to modern staging concepts.

Epidemiologically, Hodgkin lymphoma is uncommon relative to the major solid tumors, yet it remains one of the most characteristic lymphoid malignancies of adolescents and young adults. Contemporary U.S. cancer statistics estimate roughly 8,540 new Hodgkin lymphoma cases and 920 deaths in 2022, underscoring both its rarity and its generally favorable prognosis in the modern era ref [4]. A long-recognized feature is its bimodal age distribution, with an early peak in young adulthood and a later peak in older age; this pattern varies by geography, socioeconomic context, and histologic subtype, suggesting etiologic heterogeneity rather than a single uniform disease process ref [4].

Large registry and staging-series analyses further refined this epidemiologic picture. Population-based SEER data comparing 21,734 cases showed that children and adolescents differ from adults in sex balance, histologic distribution, symptom burden, and survival, with nodular sclerosis predominating in younger patients and outcomes declining with advancing age ref [5]. Detailed mapping of 719 surgically staged patients also demonstrated that mediastinal and cervical presentations are most frequent in nodular sclerosis and mixed cellularity disease, whereas lymphocyte-predominant disease shows a different pattern of presentation and spread ref [4]. Together, these historical and epidemiologic observations framed Hodgkin lymphoma as a biologically heterogeneous but clinically recognizable entity, thereby setting the stage for contemporary risk stratification and mechanism-based therapy.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Hodgkin Lymphoma: Historical Context, Etiology, and Biological Basis
subsections.content:
Compelling single-cell genotyping established that classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is, in the overwhelming majority of cases, a malignancy of mature germinal-center (GC) B cells. Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells harbor clonally rearranged and somatically mutated immunoglobulin genes, often with a shared clonal architecture across tumor cells, directly linking them to GC transit rather than to reactive bystanders ref [9], ref [7], ref [6]. Expression of the B-cell lineage factor PAX5 in Reed-Sternberg cells provided early phenotypic support for this origin despite the paradoxical loss of most conventional B-cell markers ref [8].

A central pathogenetic hallmark is the profound reprogramming of the HRS-cell transcriptional network. In many cases, immunoglobulin loci remain potentially functional, yet immunoglobulin transcription is defective, indicating that the extinguished B-cell phenotype reflects disrupted lineage maintenance rather than simple structural loss of the receptor ref [9], ref [6]. This state is reinforced by reduced or absent activity of key B-cell transcription factors such as OCT2, BOB.1/OBF.1, PU.1, and E2A, together with aberrant expression of ID2 and activation of Notch1, which collectively suppress the B-cell program and promote survival of otherwise apoptosis-prone GC B cells ref [7], ref [6].

HRS-cell survival further depends on constitutive signaling through NF-kappaB and JAK/STAT pathways. NF-kappaB activation arises through multiple, sometimes overlapping, mechanisms, including receptor signaling, EBV-encoded LMP1 in virus-positive disease, REL gains, and inactivation of negative regulators such as NFKBIA, NFKBIE, and TNFAIP3/A20 ref [7], ref [6]. EBV also has a biologically coherent role in rescuing crippled GC B cells lacking functional B-cell receptor signaling, consistent with the enrichment of EBV in cases carrying destructive immunoglobulin mutations ref [7], ref [6]. Rare exceptions exist: a small minority of cHL shows clonal T-cell receptor rearrangements and true T-cell derivation, underscoring that cHL is predominantly—but not absolutely exclusively—a GC B-cell lymphoma ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Hodgkin Lymphoma: Historical Context, Etiology, and Biological Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Pathobiology, Histologic Diversity, and Disease Classification
subsections.content:
Hodgkin lymphoma is pathobiologically defined by a minority population of malignant cells within a dominant reactive milieu, making morphology inseparable from the surrounding microenvironment in diagnosis and classification. Contemporary schemes divide the disease into classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL), the latter now increasingly recognized as biologically distinct and recently renamed nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma in updated classifications ref [12], ref [15], ref [6].

cHL accounts for about 90–95% of cases and is characterized by Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells with the canonical immunophenotype CD30-positive, usually CD15-positive, weak PAX5, and typically absent or diminished pan-B-cell markers; by contrast, NLPHL shows LP (“popcorn”) cells that retain a mature B-cell program, including CD20, CD45, BCL6, OCT2, and BOB1, and are usually CD15-/CD30- ref [12], ref [15], ref [6], ref [7]. This distinction is clinically important because NLPHL is generally more indolent, may transform to T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and can overlap morphologically with these entities ref [6], ref [7].

Histologically, cHL comprises four classic subtypes—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted—defined by architectural pattern, abundance and morphology of HRS cells, fibrosis, and inflammatory background ref [12], ref [15], ref [6]. Nodular sclerosis is the most common form in high-income settings and often presents with mediastinal disease; mixed cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted forms show stronger associations with EBV and immunodeficiency, whereas lymphocyte-rich cHL can mimic NLPHL and requires immunophenotypic resolution ref [12], ref [15], ref [6], ref [7]. Differential diagnosis also includes primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma, mediastinal gray-zone lymphoma, EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and CD30-positive T-cell lymphomas, highlighting the need for adequate excisional tissue and integrated clinicopathologic assessment ref [6], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Hodgkin Lymphoma: Historical Context, Etiology, and Biological Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Etiologic Risk Factors: Viral, Familial, and Immune Predisposition
subsections.content:
Etiologic risk in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) reflects an interplay between viral exposure, host genetics, and immune competence. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the best-established infectious factor: EBV is clonally present in Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells in a substantial subset of cHL, supporting a causal role in those tumors, and EBV-positive disease shows distinct epidemiologic patterns by age, sex, geography, and histology ref [19], ref [20]. Prior infectious mononucleosis confers an increased later risk of HL, with the association strongest for EBV-positive young-adult disease, consistent with delayed primary EBV infection as a biologically relevant antecedent ref [19], ref [20], ref [16]. Broader epidemiologic syntheses also implicate childhood environment, socioeconomic conditions, and infection-related immune maturation as modifiers of HL susceptibility ref [16].

Familial aggregation provides parallel evidence for inherited predisposition. Large registry-based analyses from the Nordic countries show an approximately threefold excess risk of cHL in first-degree relatives overall, with markedly higher risk in siblings, especially same-sex siblings and twins, and greater risk when the proband is diagnosed at a young age ref [8]. In pediatric and adolescent HL, family history of lymphoid neoplasms similarly clusters in affected pedigrees, with stronger signals for early-onset cancers and first-degree relatives ref [21]. Population-based Swedish data further support substantial familial risk across childhood through young adulthood, with hazard ratios exceeding seven for parental or sibling history of HL ref [7].

Immune predisposition is also clinically important. HL incidence is increased in settings of congenital or acquired immunodeficiency, particularly HIV infection, and HIV-associated HL is overwhelmingly EBV-positive, linking impaired immune surveillance to viral lymphomagenesis ref [20], ref [16]. Together, these observations support a model in which cHL emerges from subtype-specific combinations of EBV biology, inherited susceptibility, and altered host immune control, with important implications for risk stratification and prevention-oriented research ref [16], ref [19], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Frontline Therapeutic Strategies in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Practice Guidelines and Contemporary Frontline Treatment Frameworks
subsections.content:
Contemporary frontline management of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is fundamentally guideline-driven and stage-adapted, integrating Ann Arbor/Lugano staging, baseline risk stratification, and interim PET response assessment into therapeutic decision-making ref [22], ref [13], ref [6], ref [7]. Across major frameworks, patients are broadly separated into early-stage favorable, early-stage unfavorable/intermediate, and advanced-stage disease, although the exact definitions of bulky disease and adverse risk factors vary among NCCN, GHSG, and EORTC-based algorithms ref [22], ref [13], ref [7]. This heterogeneity is clinically important because it shapes both chemotherapy intensity and the use of consolidative radiotherapy.

In adults, current frontline frameworks retain ABVD as a global reference regimen, while PET-adapted strategies increasingly individualize treatment intensity to reduce long-term toxicity without compromising cure. For early-stage disease, combined-modality therapy remains a standard backbone, whereas omission of radiotherapy is generally restricted to carefully selected PET-negative patients after discussion of relapse risk versus late effects ref [22], ref [13], ref [6]. For advanced-stage disease, guideline-endorsed options include ABVD-based PET-adapted approaches, escalated BEACOPP in fit younger patients, and in some jurisdictions brentuximab vedotin plus AVD, reflecting divergent interpretations of efficacy-to-toxicity tradeoffs and resource availability ref [22], ref [6], ref [7]. Pre-treatment fertility counseling, cardiopulmonary assessment, and survivorship risk mitigation are therefore integral parts of the frontline framework rather than ancillary considerations ref [22], ref [13].

Pediatric and adolescent guidelines apply the same principles of risk-adapted, response-adapted therapy but place even greater emphasis on minimizing cumulative anthracycline, alkylator, bleomycin, and radiation exposure because of lifelong risks of infertility, cardiopulmonary injury, endocrinopathy, and second malignancies ref [23], ref [6]. Accordingly, contemporary frontline practice across age groups can be viewed as a continuum: cure remains the primary objective, but modern guideline architecture increasingly prioritizes biologically and imaging-informed de-escalation for low-risk responders and selective intensification for patients with higher-risk or PET-positive disease ref [22], ref [23], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Frontline Therapeutic Strategies in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
For advanced-stage adult classical Hodgkin lymphoma, frontline management has historically centered on ABVD and escalated BEACOPP, with the key trade-off being disease control versus acute and late toxicity. Long-term follow-up from GHSG HD9 showed superior tumor control and overall survival with escalated BEACOPP over COPP/ABVD, establishing the efficacy of dose-intensified therapy in high-risk disease ref [28]. However, when ABVD was compared with BEACOPP in a setting that incorporated planned high-dose salvage, BEACOPP improved initial disease control but did not confer a significant overall-survival advantage, while causing substantially greater toxicity ref [25].

These considerations drove the adoption of PET-adapted strategies. In SWOG S0816, patients with a positive interim PET after two ABVD cycles were escalated to eBEACOPP, yielding encouraging 2-year outcomes, but 5-year follow-up highlighted limitations: nearly one quarter of PET2-negative patients relapsed and second cancers were more frequent after eBEACOPP ref [8], ref [31]. Similarly, the RATHL study showed that interim PET can safely support de-escalation in PET-negative patients by omitting bleomycin after cycle 2, reducing pulmonary toxicity with only a small decrement, if any, in efficacy, while PET-positive patients treated with BEACOPP achieved intermediate long-term control ref [9]. The GITIL/FIL HD 0607 trial likewise confirmed the feasibility of switching PET2-positive patients from ABVD to escalated BEACOPP, with benefit concentrated in Deauville 4 rather than Deauville 5 disease ref [30].

More recently, incorporation of brentuximab vedotin into frontline therapy has expanded options beyond classic ABVD-versus-BEACOPP paradigms. In ECHELON-1, A+AVD improved modified progression-free survival versus ABVD in stage III/IV disease, supporting a bleomycin-sparing, antibody-drug conjugate–based approach for many adults with advanced-stage disease ref [26]. Collectively, current frontline frameworks favor individualized selection among ABVD-based, PET-adapted escalation/de-escalation, BEACOPP-based, and brentuximab-containing regimens according to relapse risk, fertility concerns, pulmonary risk, and tolerance of treatment intensity ref [25], ref [26], ref [30], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Frontline Therapeutic Strategies in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
Management of early-stage adult classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) has progressively shifted from large-field radiotherapy toward risk-adapted combined-modality therapy aimed at preserving cure while reducing late toxicity. Historical studies established that, after short-course chemotherapy, smaller radiation fields can maintain disease control: involved-field radiotherapy (IFRT) after ABVD produced long-term outcomes comparable to subtotal nodal irradiation, and in early unfavorable disease IFRT was as effective as extended-field radiotherapy with less acute toxicity, establishing field reduction as a major therapeutic advance [ref 2, ref 8].

For early unfavorable disease, combined-modality therapy remains the benchmark. In the GHSG HD11 trial, four cycles of ABVD required 30 Gy IFRT, whereas reducing radiotherapy to 20 Gy after ABVD was associated with inferior control; moderate chemotherapy intensification with BEACOPPbaseline did not clearly improve overall outcomes [ref 9]. Subsequent dose intensification in HD14 showed that two cycles of escalated BEACOPP followed by two cycles of ABVD and 30 Gy IFRT improved freedom from treatment failure and progression-free survival versus four cycles of ABVD plus 30 Gy IFRT, albeit with greater acute toxicity [ref 10].

PET-adapted de-escalation has been explored to omit radiotherapy in PET-negative patients, but randomized data have been cautionary. RAPID failed to demonstrate noninferiority for omission of radiotherapy after negative PET following three cycles of ABVD, despite excellent overall prognosis [ref 6]. Similarly, H10 and GHSG HD16 showed increased relapse risk when radiotherapy was omitted after a negative interim PET, particularly in favorable disease, while H10 also demonstrated that PET-positive patients benefit from early treatment intensification with escalated BEACOPP plus involved-node radiotherapy [ref 4, ref 5]. Collectively, these trials support contemporary practice in which favorable early-stage cHL is generally treated with abbreviated ABVD plus low-dose involved-site/involved-node radiotherapy, whereas early unfavorable disease receives combined-modality therapy with more intensive chemotherapy reserved for selected higher-risk or PET-positive patients [ref 2, ref 4, ref 6, ref 9, ref 10].

subsections.section_title: Frontline Therapeutic Strategies in Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Pediatric and Adolescent Frontline Risk-Adapted Therapy
subsections.content:
Frontline therapy for pediatric and adolescent classical Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by risk- and response-adapted treatment, with the dual aim of preserving cure while minimizing late cardiopulmonary, endocrine, fertility, and second-malignancy risks. Contemporary cooperative-group strategies stratify patients by stage, bulk, B symptoms, and increasingly interim metabolic response, allowing de-escalation of radiotherapy (RT) or chemotherapy in favorable responders and selective intensification in higher-risk subsets ref [10], ref [39], ref [44], ref [11].

In limited-stage disease, several trials established that omission of RT is feasible only in carefully selected complete responders. In GPOH-HD95, RT could be safely omitted in early-stage patients achieving strict complete remission after chemotherapy, whereas omission in intermediate-stage patients was associated with inferior progression-free survival ref [15]. Similarly, long-term follow-up of CCG 5942 showed that involved-field RT improved event-free survival after chemotherapy-induced complete response, although not overall survival, underscoring the trade-off between relapse prevention and late toxicity ref [13]. AHOD0431 further refined this paradigm in stage IA/IIA nonbulky disease, showing that nearly half of patients could receive minimal chemotherapy alone, while PET1 negativity, low ESR, and mixed-cellularity histology identified particularly favorable groups ref [44].

For intermediate- and high-risk disease, ABVE-PC–based response adaptation became a major North American platform. P9425 showed that dose-dense ABVE-PC with early response assessment yielded 5-year event-free survival of 84% while limiting cumulative anthracycline and alkylator exposure ref [10]. AHOD0031 confirmed the prognostic value of early response in intermediate-risk disease and demonstrated that rapid early responders in complete remission could omit IFRT without compromising outcome, whereas slow early responders with persistent PET positivity might benefit from augmented therapy ref [39]. In high-risk patients, AHOD0831 used PET-adapted consolidation with ifosfamide/vinorelbine for slow early responders, achieving survival comparable to prior high-risk studies despite reduced radiation volumes ref [11]. European studies likewise prioritized late-effects reduction: GPOH-HD-2002 showed that procarbazine-free OEPA-COPDAC in boys had effectiveness comparable to OPPA-COPP in girls, supporting fertility-conscious regimen design ref [45]. Most recently, AHOD1331 demonstrated improved event-free survival with brentuximab vedotin plus multiagent chemotherapy in newly diagnosed high-risk pediatric HL, signaling incorporation of targeted agents into frontline risk-adapted therapy ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Treatment-Related Toxicities, Survivorship, and Future Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Late Effects and Surveillance in Hodgkin Lymphoma Survivors
subsections.content:
Because cure rates in classical Hodgkin lymphoma are high, survivorship care must address the durable burden of treatment-related morbidity. Late effects remain clinically relevant for decades and are dominated by second malignant neoplasms and cardiovascular disease, both of which contribute substantially to excess late mortality in long-term survivors ref [47]. Risk is strongly exposure-dependent, with the highest burdens historically observed after larger-field radiotherapy, anthracycline-containing chemotherapy, and alkylator-based regimens ref [47].

Surveillance should therefore be individualized according to prior treatment fields, cumulative drug exposure, age at treatment, and sex. Women exposed to chest irradiation at a young age warrant structured early breast surveillance, while survivors treated with neck or mediastinal irradiation require ongoing assessment for thyroid dysfunction and radiation-related vascular or cardiac disease ref [47]. For patients exposed to chest radiotherapy and/or anthracyclines, long-term monitoring for coronary disease, valvular dysfunction, and heart failure is appropriate, together with aggressive management of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, obesity, and physical inactivity ref [47].

Other survivorship priorities include pulmonary toxicity after bleomycin or thoracic irradiation, fertility and gonadal dysfunction after alkylating therapy or pelvic irradiation, and less common but disabling sequelae such as chronic fatigue and neuromuscular complications ref [47]. Contemporary guidelines, including exposure-based survivorship frameworks from NCCN and the Children’s Oncology Group, support periodic history, focused examination, laboratory testing, and selected imaging rather than uniform intensive screening ref [47]. As radiation volumes shrink and novel agents enter frontline care, surveillance recommendations will need continuous recalibration to reflect changing late-effect profiles ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Treatment-Related Toxicities, Survivorship, and Future Perspectives
subsections.content:
Although most patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) are cured with first-line therapy, relapse remains the major cause of treatment failure, and outcomes after recurrence are highly heterogeneous. Early series established that the timing of relapse, presence of B symptoms, extranodal disease, and limited response to prior therapy strongly influence post-relapse survival, thereby laying the foundation for modern risk stratification in relapsed cHL ref [48]. Subsequent analyses confirmed that patients with primary refractory disease or relapse within 12 months of frontline treatment fare substantially worse than those with late relapse, particularly when recurrence is disseminated or accompanied by poor performance status.

In current practice, pre-salvage risk assessment integrates clinical course with functional imaging and transplant eligibility. PET response before autologous stem-cell transplantation (ASCT) is one of the most robust prognostic markers, with chemosensitive, PET-negative disease consistently associated with superior progression-free survival after ASCT compared with PET-positive relapse. Established adverse factors include anemia, stage IV or extranodal relapse, short remission duration, and failure to achieve metabolic complete response to salvage therapy. These variables are increasingly combined into pragmatic models to identify patients who may benefit from intensified salvage, incorporation of brentuximab vedotin or PD-1 blockade, or consideration of alternative cellular approaches rather than conventional ASCT alone.

The therapeutic landscape at relapse has also changed risk stratification by improving outcomes in biologically high-risk disease. Brentuximab vedotin has demonstrated meaningful activity both as salvage and as post-ASCT consolidation in patients with unfavorable relapse features, while PD-1 inhibitors such as nivolumab and pembrolizumab have produced high response rates in multiply relapsed disease and are being moved earlier in the salvage sequence. Accordingly, relapse assessment in cHL is evolving from a purely clinical model toward a dynamic framework that combines remission duration, disease burden, PET-defined chemosensitivity, and access to novel agents to better estimate cure probability and personalize the intensity of second-line therapy.

subsections.section_title: Treatment-Related Toxicities, Survivorship, and Future Perspectives
subsections.content:
Because cure rates in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) now exceed 80–90% in many settings, survivorship has become a central outcome, particularly for adolescents and young adults who may live for decades after treatment. Yet long-term survival is not equivalent to restoration of population-level life expectancy: excess late mortality persists and progressively shifts from relapse-related death toward treatment-related causes, especially second malignant neoplasms and cardiovascular and pulmonary disease ref [49], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

Among childhood cancer survivors, the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study demonstrated a 30-year cumulative mortality of 18.1%, with marked excess risks for death from subsequent neoplasms, cardiac disease, and pulmonary disease; radiotherapy, alkylating agents, anthracyclines, and epipodophyllotoxins were major contributors ref [49]. These patterns are highly relevant to cHL, a diagnosis historically associated with mediastinal irradiation and gonadotoxic, leukemogenic, and cardiopulmonary chemotherapy exposures. Consistently, Hodgkin lymphoma survivors show some of the highest excess risks of second cancers and cardiac mortality among childhood cancer groups, and excess mortality remains detectable for decades ref [49], ref [3], ref [5], ref [6].

Importantly, late mortality appears modifiable through treatment de-escalation and survivorship care. Reduced radiation fields and doses, anthracycline awareness, and contemporary risk-adapted strategies are expected to lessen future late deaths, although confirmation requires very long follow-up ref [2], ref [4], ref [7]. Survivorship programs should therefore integrate lifelong risk-based surveillance, cardiovascular prevention, screening for breast, lung, thyroid, and gastrointestinal malignancies when appropriate, fertility and endocrine follow-up, and attention to psychosocial and health-behavior determinants that may further shape long-term mortality ref [5], ref [8], ref [9].
